title: Contrast — Image Wiki
text:
Contrast
  Difference — how much a part of a picture differs from what sits next to it. An edge exists only where something changes, so contrast is what makes anything visible at all.

  
    Termcontrast
    Also calledtonal contrast, value contrast, colour contrast, difference
    Not the same assaturation, brightness, dynamic range, sharpness
    Read8 min
  

  
    
      On this page
      
        Why it happensIt is local, and it is relativeThe axes it can run onContrast spends attentionCommon mistakes
      
    
  

  Look at this page: dark letters, pale background. Now imagine turning the difference between the two down, step by step. The words do not get harder to read the way small type is harder to read. At some point they stop existing.
Hold a hand up against a bright window and you get the same lesson from the other side. No knuckles, no fingernails, no colour — a hand-shaped hole. All the difference in that view sits between the hand and the sky, and none of it is inside the hand.
Contrast is difference. That is the whole definition, and everything useful follows from one consequence of it: an edge exists only where something changes. Where nothing changes there is no edge, and where there is no edge there is no shape. Hierarchy, balance, a subject that reads at thumbnail size — all of it is built on differences somebody could see.
Why it happens
Your eye is not a light meter, it is a difference detector, and it is aggressive about the job. David Briggs's summary of the research states the machine's priorities in one sentence: vision goes looking for edges, uses those edges as the borders of areas, then suppresses variation inside each area and enhances the contrast between them (SRC-064).
The second half is the surprising part. The eye does not merely report differences, it exaggerates them at boundaries and invents them where none exist. Print a row of grey bars each about three lightness steps darker than the last and the flat bars will look fluted, each one carrying a bright fringe along one side and a dark fringe along the other — Mach bands, and none of that fringing is in the ink. In the Cornsweet figure two areas of identical grey look plainly different because a graded edge between them propagates inward (SRC-064).
So contrast is not only a property of the picture. Part of it is manufactured by the person looking, at the boundaries.
It is local, and it is relative

patch #8A8F98 · ground #101216A light shapea moth on a night windowthe patch is the brightest thing herepatch #8A8F98 · ground #8A8F98No shape at alla grey coat against a grey wallthe dashes mark where it still ispatch #8A8F98 · ground #F7F8FAA dark shapea pigeon on fresh snowthe patch is the darkest thing here

The square is the same colour in all three panels — #8A8F98, unchanged, not adjusted, not relit. Only the ground behind it differs.
On the left it is the brightest thing in the frame and reads as a light shape. On the right it is the darkest thing in the frame and reads as a dark shape. In the middle it is nothing at all: the ground has been set to the square's own value and the shape stops existing, which is why the dashes are there to show you where it still is.
Nothing about the square changed across those three panels. Everything about how it reads did.


This is why two instructions people use interchangeably are not the same instruction. "Make it brighter" changes one number. "Make it stand out" changes a relationship, and you can do it by lowering the neighbours instead — usually the cheaper move, because raising the subject means adding brightness or colour that then has to compete with everything else in the frame that is already bright and colourful (SRC-031).
The axes it can run on
Value is the strongest by a distance, but it is not the only channel. Design writing lists the properties you can push as size, colour, value, texture, shape and orientation, with density and depth of field on top (SRC-030); Getty's definition of emphasis is the same idea from the other end — one area is made to stand out by differing from the others in size, colour, texture or shape (SRC-002).

Value — light against dark. Survives squinting, thumbnails and greyscale. See Value structure.
Hue — red against green. Loud, and much weaker than it feels.
Chroma — one saturated note in a grey field. See Hue, value and chroma.
Size — one big thing among small ones. Real but overrated on its own.
Shape — a circle among rectangles, a curve among straight lines.
Texture — smooth against rough, plain against patterned.
Sharpness — a crisp region inside a blurred one. The reason shallow focus points.
Direction — one diagonal in a field of verticals.
Density — a crowded patch beside an empty one, with no single element doing the work.



Two values and nothing between them: Vallotton, La Manifestation, 1893
Almost no value difference anywhere: Turner, Norham Castle, Sunrise, c. 1845


Félix Vallotton, La Manifestation (The Demonstration), 1893, woodcut (National Gallery of Art, CC0). J. M. W. Turner, Norham Castle, Sunrise, c. 1845 (Tate). Public domain.
Vallotton has exactly two values: black ink and cream paper. No greys, no modelling, no gradient anywhere. And nothing is unclear — you can read coats, a checked scarf, a dropped top hat, a bare shoulder, a crowd in flight. Contrast at its maximum needs no help from anything else.
Turner works at the other extreme. Sky, water, mist and stone all sit in the top third of the value scale; the castle is a soft blue-grey mass you have to hunt for, and the horizon is a guess. With value nearly switched off, the picture leans on the two axes it has left: the small cow at the front is the only strongly coloured thing in the frame, and the sun's glow is the only concentration of anything. Both hold, but only just — and both would vanish in a bad greyscale conversion.





Vincent van Gogh, The Night Café, September 1888 (Yale University Art Gallery). Public domain.
Van Gogh described this room to his brother as an attempt to say something with red and green, and the hue difference he built is about as large as paint allows: blood-red walls against a green ceiling and a green billiard table.
Now squint at it. Almost all of that difference disappears. The room collapses into a light floor, a darker everything-above, and four bright lamps — because the reds and the greens, however far apart in hue, sit close together in value. Ask where your eye actually goes: the lamps, then the pale figure by the table. Both are value events. The hue is doing the mood; the drawing is being done by four small patches of light.


Contrast spends attention
Attention is a fixed budget and contrast is how you spend it. Which means it can be overspent, and there is a stock complaint that describes exactly that: it looks busy.

ringed: the same mark, #1B1E25, in both panelsOne mark is differenteleven neighbours agree on a pale valueyou found it before you looked for itringed: the same mark, #1B1E25, in both panelsEvery mark is differentthe same eleven neighbours, now all loudyou have to search, and it is no longer first

Twelve marks in both panels, in the same twelve positions. The ringed mark is identical in both — same size, same place, same #1B1E25.
On the left it wins without a fight, because its eleven neighbours agreed on one value and it did not. On the right the neighbours were given loud values of their own, and the ringed mark has lost. Nothing was taken away from it. Dominance is a comparison, and it now loses several of them (SRC-031).
That is the mechanism behind contrast everywhere is contrast nowhere. It is also why the fix for a subject that will not stand out is usually somewhere else in the frame — see Simplification.


Design practice settles on about three distinguishable levels of emphasis: one dominant thing, a few focal points, and a background that recedes. Push past that and each new level eats the difference between its neighbours (SRC-031). Photography Life's version, from the field rather than the page, is that high and low contrast are two moods rather than a good setting and a bad one — high contrast reads intense, low contrast reads quiet, and neither is a score (SRC-021).
Common mistakes

"More contrast is better." Contrast is a currency, not a quality. Raising it everywhere raises the noise floor and buys nothing, because what you needed was one difference bigger than the others.
"High contrast means bright." It means a big gap between neighbours. A picture can be dark overall and enormously contrasty, or blazingly bright and almost flat.
"Contrast means the slider in the editor." That slider stretches the whole tonal range at once. The contrast that decides whether a subject reads is between a shape and the few centimetres around it.
"These colours are completely different, so the shapes will separate." Only if they differ in value. Equal-value colours give the weakest edge there is.
"Contrast and dynamic range are the same thing." Range is what the medium can record between its darkest and brightest; contrast is how far apart you put things inside it.


Reading contrast in five seconds

Squint until detail goes. What still separates from its surroundings? That is the contrast that is actually working.
Name the axis. Is that difference value, hue, chroma, size, texture, sharpness — or several stacked in one place?
Check the neighbours, not the whole frame. Is the subject different from what touches it, or only from the far corner?
Count the loud areas. More than three and you no longer have a hierarchy, you have a crowd.
If the subject is weak, ask what you could turn down before you ask what to turn up.



  
    
      Read next
      
        
          
            
              Value structure
              How light or dark things are, independent of their colour. Squint at any image and what survives is its value structure — and if that does not read, no colour will save it.
            
          
        
          
            
              Visual hierarchy
              The order in which your eye visits the parts of an image — decided by the image, not by you.
            
          
        
          
            
              Hue, value and chroma
              A colour is not one thing. It is three independent dials — which colour it is, how light it is, and how far it sits from grey — and most arguments about colour are two people turning different dials.
            
          
        
          
            
              Simplification
              Every element you add divides the viewer's attention, so the question about anything in the frame is never whether it is nice but what it is doing. Taking things out is the hardest edit there is.
